title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and exposing private data, report says
content:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.
In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.
One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.
Meta did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

report.summary: Meta’s AI agent Muse reportedly mixed conversations across accounts and exposed private data, triggering internal privacy concerns despite rapid growth.
report.background: Muse launched in September and has surpassed 10 million downloads, making it one of the fastest-growing apps on record. It is part of a broader industry push toward AI agents that can act across messages, calendars, shopping, and financial apps. That cross-app access and persistent memory are what make agents useful, but they also create hard engineering and governance problems: isolating each user’s data, enforcing consent, and preventing one account’s context from bleeding into another. Reuters reported that Meta employees raised concerns in internal posts about mixed conversations and exposed data; Meta did not immediately comment to TechCrunch. The episode lands as rivals race to ship agents and regulators scrutinize AI privacy.
key_points: Employees described Muse surfacing content that did not belong to them, including childcare requests, career advice, product orders and bank balances. In one internal example, a weather-and-tide chat suddenly included Capital One and Charles Schwab balances. That suggests failures in account isolation or context routing, not just a harmless glitch.

Another employee said Muse reminded her to reply to a Signal message from her sister on her personal phone, even though she did not grant access to other apps. If accurate, it points to over-broad permissions or background data access that users did not clearly consent to.

The concerns were reportedly raised in internal company posts and covered by Reuters. Meta did not immediately respond to TechCrunch. The lack of public explanation leaves open whether the issue is limited, fixed, or systemic.

Muse’s scale raises the stakes: more than 10 million downloads since September means small isolation bugs can become mass privacy incidents. Fast adoption also pressures teams to ship personalization before permission controls and audit trails mature.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Muse is a warning that agent credibility depends less on model quality than on permission architecture. Cross-account leakage can trigger regulatory scrutiny and erode trust in all assistants. Developers should treat memory as sensitive data, enforce per-user isolation, log data provenance, request explicit consent for app access, and test for cross-tenant leakage before launch. Regular users should review which apps and data an agent can reach, avoid granting blanket access, and treat unsolicited personal details as a red flag. The incident may slow feature rollouts but could push the industry toward clearer consent and audit standards.
report.tools: For follow-up, watch open-source agent frameworks with scoped memory and tracing, such as LangGraph, Microsoft AutoGen and CrewAI; use Microsoft Presidio for PII detection and redaction; add OpenTelemetry for audit logs. OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications is a useful threat-modeling checklist for agent privacy risks.
